---
title: "Parallel Iterators with Rayon"
---

# Parallel Iterators with Rayon

`rayon` splits a slice across a thread pool and joins the results. The adaptors look like `Iterator`. They are a different trait, `ParallelIterator`, and the closures have stricter bounds: they must be `Send` and `Sync` as the trait demands, because another thread may run them.

```toml
[dependencies]
rayon = "1.10"
```

## The concept

`par_iter` borrows items in parallel. `into_par_iter` moves them. `map` and `filter` stay lazy until a consumer such as `sum`, `collect`, `reduce`, or `for_each`. The order of side effects is not the source order. The order of `collect` into a `Vec` is the source order. Rayon pays the pool and the join. Short slices are slower in parallel than in series.

## Recipe 55 — Drop-in parallelism with par_iter()

```rust
fn main() {
    use rayon::prelude::*;

    let readings: Vec<i32> = (0..10_000).collect();
    let serial: i64 = readings.iter().map(|n| i64::from(*n) * 2).sum();
    let parallel: i64 = readings.par_iter().map(|n| i64::from(*n) * 2).sum();
    assert_eq!(serial, parallel);
}
```

`par_iter` yields `&i32`, same as `iter`. The `map` closure is `Fn` and `Send`. Capturing a thread-local or a non-`Sync` cell will not compile, and that is the point.

## Recipe 56 — Parallel aggregation with reduce() and sum()

`sum` is the right consumer for addition. `reduce` is the consumer when the operation is your own, and it must be associative. Parallel `reduce` combines partial results in an unspecified order.

```rust
fn main() {
    use rayon::prelude::*;

    let readings: Vec<i32> = (1..=100).collect();
    let by_sum: i32 = readings.par_iter().copied().sum();
    let by_reduce = readings.par_iter().copied().reduce(|| 0, |acc, n| acc + n);
    assert_eq!(by_sum, 5050);
    assert_eq!(by_reduce, 5050);
}
```

The first closure of `reduce` builds an identity for a split that has no items. Addition's identity is `0`. Subtraction is not associative. Do not `reduce` with subtraction and expect the serial answer.

`max` is associative for this purpose. An empty iterator has no max, so use a form that allows "no value":

```rust
fn main() {
    use rayon::prelude::*;

    let readings = [3, 9, 4, 9, 1];
    let max = readings.par_iter().copied().max();
    assert_eq!(max, Some(9));
}
```

## Recipe 57 — Parallel flat_map and collecting into a HashMap

`flat_map_iter` flattens a normal iterator, such as `str::split`, under a parallel outer iterator. `flat_map` would require that inner iterator to be parallel itself. `collect` into a `HashMap` is implemented for pairs. Keys that collide keep one value. Which duplicate survives is not worth depending on. Deduplicate before the parallel step if the winner matters.

```rust
fn main() {
    use rayon::prelude::*;
    use std::collections::HashMap;

    let lines = ["ada,linus", "grace", "ada"];
    let names: Vec<&str> = lines
        .par_iter()
        .flat_map_iter(|line| line.split(','))
        .collect();
    names.iter().for_each(|name| assert!(!name.is_empty()));
    assert_eq!(names.len(), 4);

    let lengths: HashMap<&str, usize> = ["ada", "linus", "grace"]
        .par_iter()
        .map(|name| (*name, name.len()))
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(lengths.get("linus"), Some(&5));
}
```

`collect` into `Vec` from `flat_map` preserves order in rayon. The `HashMap` does not have a useful order. Look up by key.

## Recipe 58 — Knowing when not to use Rayon

Parallelism loses when each item is tiny and there are few of them, and when the body must run in source order or on the calling thread.

```rust
fn main() {
    use rayon::prelude::*;

    let small = [1, 2, 3, 4];
    let serial: i32 = small.iter().map(|n| n + 1).sum();
    let parallel: i32 = small.par_iter().map(|n| n + 1).sum();
    assert_eq!(serial, parallel);
}
```

The results match. The parallel call still started the pool's bookkeeping. For four additions that is a net loss. Reach for `par_iter` when you have a large slice and the per-item work is enough to hide the join: parsing, compression, image pixels, a non-trivial numeric kernel. Keep `iter` for short slices, for I/O that is already buffered on one file, and for any loop that `break`s on the first failure in order. Parallel iterators do not `break` the way `for` does. `try_for_each` can stop early, and in-flight items still finish.
